items.prompt: What actually sets off the body changes of puberty?

options.label: A sudden growth of the bones themselves, with no other cause
options.feedback: Bones do not start this process on their own. Something else has to switch them on first.

options.label: A change in diet that happens automatically with age
options.feedback: Diet can support growth, but it is not the trigger that starts puberty in the first place.

options.label: A signal from the brain that ramps up hormone production
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: Muscles reaching a certain size on their own
options.feedback: Muscle size is a result of these changes, not the cause that starts them.

items.ok_line: A brain signal starts a chain that reaches the whole body.
items.ko_line: None of these body parts start this process on their own — something has to switch them on first.
items.exp_title: A signal that starts a chain reaction
items.exp_text: A region deep in the brain begins releasing a hormone that tells glands elsewhere in the body to ramp up production of their own hormones. Those rising hormone levels then travel through the bloodstream and set off the whole cascade of changes that make up puberty.

items.prompt: During the adolescent growth spurt, do all parts of the body lengthen at the same time?

options.label: Yes, every bone lengthens at exactly the same pace
options.feedback: Growth is not evenly spread across the body during this stage. Some parts noticeably outpace others.

options.label: No — the torso lengthens first, then the legs catch up later
options.feedback: The order runs the other way around during this stage.

options.label: No — only the arms grow during this stage
options.feedback: The arms are not singled out this way. Growth is spread unevenly across several parts of the body, not confined to the arms alone.

options.label: No — the legs typically lengthen first, with the torso catching up after
options.feedback: Correct.

items.ok_line: Legs first, torso catching up afterward.
items.ko_line: Growth during this stage is noticeably uneven across the body. Think about which parts tend to lead.
items.exp_title: Growth that arrives out of order
items.exp_text: When the growth spurt begins, the legs are usually the first part of the body to lengthen quickly, followed some months later by the torso. That staggered order can leave a teenager's proportions looking briefly mismatched before the rest of the body catches up.

items.prompt: Why do a teenager's hands and feet sometimes seem to grow before the rest of the body catches up?

options.label: The bones in the hands and feet tend to reach their adult size earlier in the growth spurt
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: Shoes and gloves stretch them out of shape
options.feedback: Footwear and gloves do not reshape bones. The bones themselves are genuinely growing on their own schedule.

options.label: They are not actually growing faster; it is an illusion caused by clothing
options.feedback: This is a real, measurable pattern in bone growth, not simply an appearance created by clothing.

options.label: Hands and feet stop growing earliest of all, making them look larger by comparison
options.feedback: They are not the first to stop growing. They are actually among the first to speed up and reach their fuller size.

items.ok_line: Hands and feet often lead the way in a growth spurt.
items.ko_line: This is a real, measurable pattern in bone growth, not something caused by clothing.
items.exp_title: Growth that arrives at the extremities first
items.exp_text: During the growth spurt, the bones of the hands and feet tend to reach a larger share of their eventual adult size earlier than the long bones of the arms and legs. That earlier growth is why a teenager's shoe size can jump well ahead of the rest of their height.

items.prompt: What causes a boy's voice to deepen during puberty?

options.label: The lungs grow larger and push more air out
options.feedback: Bigger lungs would change breath capacity, not the pitch of a voice, which comes from a different part of the body.

options.label: The larynx grows and the vocal cords inside it lengthen and thicken
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: The mouth and jaw grow wider, changing the sound
options.feedback: Jaw shape can affect how sound is shaped in the mouth, but the pitch itself is set further down, in the throat.

options.label: The vocal cords shrink and vibrate less
options.feedback: Shrinking cords vibrating less would raise pitch, not lower it. What actually happens is closer to the opposite.

items.ok_line: A larger voice box means longer, thicker cords, and a lower pitch.
items.ko_line: Pitch is set by a structure in the throat, not by the lungs or the shape of the mouth.
items.exp_title: A larger box, a lower note
items.exp_text: Hormones during puberty cause the larynx, the box of cartilage in the throat that holds the vocal cords, to grow noticeably larger, especially in boys. As it grows, the vocal cords inside stretch longer and thicken, and longer, thicker cords vibrate more slowly, producing a lower pitch.

items.prompt: Why does height growth eventually come to an end after adolescence?

options.label: The bones simply run out of calcium
options.feedback: A shortage of calcium would weaken bone, but it is not what actually stops height growth at the end of adolescence.

options.label: Muscles stop stretching, holding the bones back
options.feedback: Muscles adjust to whatever length the bones reach; they are not what determines when bones stop lengthening.

options.label: The growth plates turn into solid bone and can no longer add length
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: The body decides a person is tall enough and stops signaling
options.feedback: There is no such decision being made. What stops growth is a physical change in the bone itself.

items.ok_line: The zone that once added length turns solid.
items.ko_line: Think back to the strip of cartilage responsible for adding length to a bone, and what eventually happens to it.
items.exp_title: A cartilage strip that closes for good
items.exp_text: The growth plates that once produced new bone at the ends of the long bones gradually run out of the cartilage-forming cells that keep them active. Once that cartilage layer is fully replaced by solid bone, the plate closes and that bone can no longer add any further length.

items.prompt: What triggers the growth of new body hair during puberty?

options.label: Friction from clothing stimulates the follicles
options.feedback: Rubbing from clothing does not switch on hair follicles. The trigger comes from inside the body instead.

options.label: Cold weather activates dormant follicles
options.feedback: Temperature is not what wakes these follicles up. A change inside the body is responsible.

options.label: Hair follicles simply age and start producing hair on a timer
options.feedback: It is not simple aging on a fixed timer. A specific internal change is what switches these follicles on.

options.label: Rising hormone levels switch on follicles that were dormant before
options.feedback: Correct.

items.ok_line: Follicles that were dormant get switched on by hormones.
items.ko_line: Nothing about the surrounding weather or clothing turns these follicles on. Look inside the body instead.
items.exp_title: Follicles waiting to be switched on
items.exp_text: Many hair follicles across the body are present long before puberty but stay dormant, producing only very fine, faint hair. Rising hormone levels during puberty make those follicles sensitive to the signal, switching them into producing thicker, longer hair in places like the underarms and elsewhere.

items.prompt: Why does skin often become oilier during puberty?

options.label: Hormones make the skin's oil glands more active
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: Sweating increases and leaves an oily residue
options.feedback: Sweat itself is watery, not oily. A different kind of gland is responsible for the oil on the skin's surface.

options.label: The skin's surface layer thins out and lets oil through
options.feedback: The skin's outer layer does not thin out at this stage. The change is in how much oil is being produced, not in what can pass through.

options.label: New oil glands form for the first time
options.feedback: The glands are already present well before puberty. What changes is how active they become, not whether they exist.

items.ok_line: The same glands as before, working harder under a hormone signal.
items.ko_line: The glands responsible for skin oil already exist well before puberty. Ask what changes their activity level.
items.exp_text: Small glands attached to hair follicles across the skin produce an oily substance that keeps the skin and hair from drying out. Rising hormone levels during puberty make those glands produce noticeably more of that oil than before, which is why skin often becomes shinier and more prone to blocked pores at this stage.

items.prompt: Why does body odor typically change and become stronger during puberty?

options.label: The skin stops washing itself as effectively
options.feedback: Skin does not have a self-cleaning process that could stop working. The change comes from a gland becoming active instead.

options.label: A type of sweat gland found mainly in the armpits and groin becomes active
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: Sweat itself changes from being watery to being oily
options.feedback: The watery sweat produced across most of the skin does not turn oily. A separate, different kind of gland is what changes at this stage.

options.label: Existing sweat glands simply produce more of the same sweat
options.feedback: It is not just more of the same fluid. A different type of gland, largely inactive before puberty, starts working for the first time.

items.ok_line: A separate gland switches on, not just more of the usual sweat.
items.ko_line: A specific kind of gland, concentrated in a few areas of the body, is what becomes active here.
items.exp_title: A second kind of sweat gland waking up
items.exp_text: Most of the skin is covered in glands that produce a thin, watery sweat for cooling, but a second kind of gland, clustered in the armpits and groin, stays largely inactive until puberty. Once hormones switch that second kind on, it releases a thicker fluid that bacteria on the skin break down, producing the stronger odor associated with puberty.

items.prompt: What is likely happening in the body when a growing teenager gets aching pains in the legs at night?

options.label: The bones are cracking under the strain of growth
options.feedback: Growing bone is not cracking. The ache comes from surrounding tissue rather than damage to the bone itself.

options.label: The blood supply to the legs is temporarily cut off
options.feedback: Blood flow to the legs is not interrupted during growth. The discomfort has a different, more mechanical cause.

options.label: The bones are lengthening a little faster than the surrounding muscles and tendons can keep up
options.feedback: Correct.

options.label: The muscles are shrinking as the bones lengthen
options.feedback: Muscles are not shrinking during a growth spurt. If anything, they are being stretched and having to lengthen themselves.

items.ok_line: Bone briefly outpaces the muscle and tendon stretching to match it.
items.ko_line: Nothing is being damaged or cut off here. Think about the pace mismatch between bone and the tissue around it.
items.exp_title: A pace mismatch, not an injury
items.exp_text: During a growth spurt, the bones can lengthen slightly faster than the muscles and tendons attached to them are able to stretch and grow in response. That extra pull on tissue still catching up is thought to be behind the aching many teenagers feel in their legs, often worse at night when the legs have been still for a while.

items.prompt: Why do many teenagers go through a temporarily clumsy phase during a growth spurt?

options.label: Their muscles genuinely weaken while bones lengthen
options.feedback: Muscles are not actually getting weaker during this stage. The problem lies in coordination, not in strength.

options.label: Their eyesight changes suddenly during this stage
options.feedback: A sudden shift in eyesight is not behind this clumsiness. The mismatch is between limb length and the brain's sense of the body, not vision.

options.label: Bones stop responding to signals from the brain for a while
options.feedback: Bones do not receive or lose signals from the brain in this way. The issue involves the brain's internal map of the body, not the bones directly.

options.label: Limbs lengthen faster than the brain's sense of the body's size can keep up with
options.feedback: Correct.

items.ok_line: Limbs change size faster than the brain's map of them updates.
items.ko_line: Nothing here is about lost strength or lost signals. Think about how the brain keeps track of limb length, and how quickly that tracking can update.
items.exp_title: A map that lags behind the body
items.exp_text: The brain relies on a constantly updated internal sense of how long each limb is in order to judge distances and movements accurately. When a growth spurt lengthens arms and legs quickly, that internal sense takes a while to catch up, so reaches and steps are briefly misjudged until the brain's map adjusts to the new proportions.
